Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. Last Sunday as I was driving to Montreal, two policemen were stopping all traffic just outside the city limits. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the Minister of Justice yet in a position to answer the questions put to him on Saturday about the questionnaire being circulated in certain departments of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO QUESTIONNAIRE CIRCULATED IN CERTAIN DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
I am prepared to answer that question; in fact, I have been seeking an opportunity for the last few minutes.
With reference to the questions asked on Saturday, June 19, by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the government are aware of the concern felt by members generally in the matter of the security of government employees. For that reason it is felt to be advisable that a general statement on the subject should be made.
The government is acutely aware of its responsibility in relation to security within the government service, and administrative measures have been taken to ensure the safety of the state in this respect. These measures do not interfere with traditional principles of just treatment.
In the government's view, loyalty is not susceptible to any precise series of tests. Accordingly, after careful consideration, it was decided not to set up an elaborate organization, as had been done elsewhere, to determine and adjudicate upon the loyalty of government employees. As was indicated to the House of Commons by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) on April 14, 1947 (Hansard, page 1993), an interdepartmental panel on security, composed of officials from departments and agencies of government, was set up some time ago to advise on the coordination of the planning, organization and execution of security measures generally which affect government departments. These measures necessarily include the devising of the best methods of carrying out inquiries concerning applicants for government employment in order to determine their suitability from a security point of view. The security panel advises on measures and methods. It does not deal with individual cases.
With regard to the so-called questionnaires, there are, of course, a number of forms used by departments for ordinary administrative purposes as a necessary part of their personnel management. In addition, forms are in use in some departments for the purpose of assembling relevant information concerning persons whose duties include work of a secret character. The use of these so-called questionnaires for security purposes is merely a means of facilitating the work of those who have to make the necessary inquiries. They are employed only for persons in positions of trust and not for the great majority of government employees. In some cases the information required can be and is obtained from departmental personnel records and from the records of the civil service commission. In other cases, the information is requested
5630	COMMONS
Department of National Defence Act
of the employees themselves by means of questionnaires. The completion of such forms is not compulsory. They are designed to help those responsible to obtain quickly information which may be helpful in- assessing the suitability of individuals for confidential employment. Incidentally, departmental practice in this respect is under review and I can assure the house that any Objectionable and unnecessary features in such documents, such as questions concerning collateral relatives and any irrelevant inquiry into the private lives of individuals, will not be permitted.
The government is of the opinion that loyalty to the state of employees in positions 6f trust is an essential aspect of the efficient conduct of public administration. Moreover, there are certain duties of such a secret character that the state would not be justified in employing for their performance any person whose trustworthiness is in doubt.
Under the terms of the Civil Service Act and regulations, the civil service commission is required to satisfy itself as to the character and habits of persons appointed by it to government employment. These provisions do not apply to all employees or departments and agencies, nor do they relieve departments of their responsibility for satisfying themselves as to the suitability of individual employees from a security standpoint.
The particular attention of heads of departments and agencies of government has been drawn to their responsibility with respect to the reliability of employees under their charge from the security point of view. A procedure has been approved which will enable them to discharge this responsibility as a part of their normal administrative function.
This is the position of the government with respect to security in relation to government employees generally. There is, however, the special case of those who are members of or associated with the communist party. The government is satisfied, from all the evidence available, that it would be a risk to the security of the state to employ such persons in positions of trust. For this reason, and in the discharge of its primary responsibility for security, the government has decided that no person who is a member of the communist party or associated with it shall be employed in work of a secret character. I may add that the same rule applies to those associated with fascist organizations.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932, AND FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 350, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932, and the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps a brief word of explanation of this bill should be made.
The first purpose of the bill is to enlarge the powers of Canadian, insurance companies to permit them to invest in mortgages in excess of the usual limit of 60 per cent of the appraised value, where the excess is guaranteed by the government of the province of Ontario under the authority of The Housing Development Ac't, 1948, passed at the la^t session of the Ontario legislature.
At the present time there is authority in The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932, for making investment in so-called "excess" mortgages, but only in cases where the excess is insured by the federal housing administrator of the United States of America. The experience under this type of mortgage has been so good that it is considered justifiable to substitute a more general provision for the existing one. The new provision will enable tire companies to participate in the Ontario scheme, or any similar national, provincial or State schemes in countries where they are carrying on business, and in so doing to take advantage of sound investment opportunities.
The second purpose of it he bill is to enlarge to a limited extent the general investment powers of Canadian insurance companies. The steady increase in the funds 'to be invested by the companies has been accompanied by increasing difficulty in finding suitable investments within the prescribed classes. This problem has been the subject of discussion between representatives of the companies and officials of the department of insurance from time to time, but more extensively during the last few months. While the principle of restricting the investments of insurance companies to specified classes is unquestionably desirable, nevertheless new types of sound investments not within the prescribed classes are continually
coming into existence, very often in limited amounts, and frequently the best of them are available for only a short time before being taken up by other investors-sometimes by British and foreign insurance companies possessing wider investment powers. This situation 'has pointed to the desirability of granting to Canadian insurance companies a small degree of freedom in their investment powers, subject always to certain general prohibitions and restrictions, and the effect of subsection 3 of section 1 of the bill is to permit relative freedom up to a limit of three per cent of a company's total assets.
When it is remembered that British insurance companies have practically one hundred per cent freedom, and that their record stands as an example to the insurance world, the proposed limit of three per cent for Canadian companies appears to be reasonable and justifiable. Another consideration pointing to a provision of this kind is that the merits of different investments within a particular class vary greatly, and while some of them may undoubtedly be first grade, it might be unsatisfactory in some cases to authorize specifically that particular class as a whole. In addition, it is becoming more difficult to prescribe satisfactory tests for certain desirable investments.
The record of Canadian insurance company management is such as to merit confidence that the additional powers here conferred will be exercised in the best interests of the policyholders. It is a minor change in the investment powers. I would not undertake to make any substantial change without a great deal more study on the part of the department of insurance to the whole question of insurance companies' investment power.

speechtext:
Mr. GLEASON BELZILE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 351, to amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Loans without collateral security.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LOANS WITHOUT COLLATERAL SECURITY, ETC.
speechtext: Will the parliamentary assistant make a statement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LOANS WITHOUT COLLATERAL SECURITY, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps a brief statement would be in order so as to give the committee some information on the subject.
This bill was introduced in the senate, and it pertains to the Quebec savings banks. The Quebec savings banks are institutions operating under special charters. There are two of them, both operating in that province.
In 1846 the Montreal City and District Savings Bank was founded. Its charter was granted by the Dominion of Canada in 1871. This savings bank operates only in the city and district of Montreal, where it has its head office and twenty-five branches. It has some
300,000	depositors.
The Quebec Savings Bank, or La Basque d'Economie de Quebec, was founded in 1848. It was incorporated in 1855 by an act of the Canadian legislature, and given a dominion charter by 34 Victoria, chapter 7. The Quebec Savings Bank operates only in the city and district of Quebec where it has fourteen branches.
These two banks are real savings banks; that is, they were established for the promotion of thrift and to encourage the regular saving of small amounts. The scope of their operations is limited to receiving deposits, investing them in gilt-edged securities, and granting loans guaranteed by the same kind of securities. They do not cater to the ordinary commercial risks. A clause in their charters stipulates that they must confine their operations to the accommodation of the non-business class of depositors.
There is no service charge of any kind for the granting of loans or for the opening and maintenance of accounts, and clients may issue cheques against their accounts.
For the convenience of their clients, the offices or branches of these banks are kept open to business on week-day evenings. It has been found that the great majority of the clients of

Quebec Savings Banks Act
these banks are of the working class particularly, and that they deposit small weekly or monthly amounts out of their pay cheques. It has been established that they seldom use their savings for ordinary purposes, but that, on the contrary, they will use them only in emergencies such as death, illness, or in special circumstances such as the purchase of a house, outlays for education of children, and the like.
The provisions of their charters and of the act place severe restrictions on the investments which these banks are allowed to make. Section 35, as it now stands, provides that these banks may invest moneys only in bonds, debentures, or other securities of or guaranteed by the government of Canada, or by provincial governments of Canada; in municipal bonds or debentures of school corporations in Canada, or bonds and debentures guaranteed by the United Kingdom, and so on. There is even a provision which makes it an offence and imposes a heavy penalty if the banks place money in unauthorized investments.
Section 37 provides that the banks may not lend any money upon the personal security of individuals, or to corporate bodies without collateral securities up to the amount of the loan, and these collaterals must be only certain kinds of bonds. Furthermore, the provisions of section 39 prohibit the making of a loan upon the security of real or immovable property.
The result has been that these restrictions are so great that the banks cannot actually meet the desires of their clients as to personal or mortgage loans. This bill would remedy this situation and permit the banks to make unsecured personal loans to a client, not exceeding at any time the amount of $1,000, and the aggregate amount of these loans made by the banks are not, at any time, to exceed five per cent of their deposit liabilities. It will further enable the banks to grant such loans on first mortgage on improved property, provided that such loans do not exceed sixty per cent of the value of the mortgaged property; and here again the aggregate amount of these loans shall not exceed five per cent of the deposit liabilities of the lending bank.
These powers to be conferred on these banks are not unlimited, as will be seen by the short explanation which has been given. They would be, in fact, similar to the powers of the trust companies and conform with the provisions of the civil code of the province of Quebec, section 981 o, as to the administration of funds by a trustee, tutor or curator.
It has been deemed necessary to permit the enlargement of the powers of the banks in
order to give them an opportunity to get their funds into more profitable circulation. These banks are well-managed institutions. Their losses have been few and far between, because they make only loans containing a minimum of risk.
The bill contains some minor amendments to bring the act into line with the Income Tax Act and with the Bank Act, and certain provisions relating to income and investment reports to be made to the Minister of Finance. But the main purpose of the bill is to empower these banks to render additional services to the public in general.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.

The Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue will collect such taxes as, in the discretion of his department, may seem proper. But here we find something totally different. We find a government official determining when a surplus should cease to be a surplus, and I submit that this government official does not know. He has not the training or the experience to determine what, in the circumstances of any particular case, should be the reserve necessary for the protection. and w'ell-being of the institution. The government official is not responsible to anybody for the sufficiency of protection for the shareholders and depositors of a bank, especially a savings bank.
The other day, as a matter of policy, at the decree of the government or one of its creatures, interest rates went up and the market price of bonds fell. Institutions such as these, and others, saw their reserves impinged upon to the extent of thousands or hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars. How helpless is the institution in the face of conditions over which it has no control; yet this act will deny an institution the right to determine what safety measures should be taken against these unknown and all-pervading influences of uncertainty and chaos.
I cannot but express my profound regret that the government has found it necessary to assume a further measure of control over a purely domestic institution, well administered, concerning which there is no control and no complaint. So far as I am concerned there is no reason for the enactment of this amendment, unless it be to enable the government further to determine what shall be, in the realm of what used to be free enterprise.

I should like to make it clear that in order to get the benefit of the British preferential rates it will still be necessary for goods to be shipped direct from the originating country to a sea, lake or river port of Canada. The new section simply provides that goods bona fide exported to Canada from any country, but passing in transit through another, shall, upon such terms and conditions as to shipment, documentation, warehousing, transhipment or the like as the governor in council may prescribe, be valued for duty as if they were imported from the first-mentioned country. The change by the new section gives direct statutory authority for such valuation rather than merely empowering the governor in council to make such a provision.
The terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council under both the existing and the new section have been and would be such as are required to establish shipment from the original country destined to Canada, and preclude abuse. In other words, shipment from the original country when destined to Canada would require to be established by the documents. As a general rule, warehousing or remaining in an intermediate country for any purpose other than that of transhipment would void direct shipment from the originating country, and the new section makes no real change in the administration in this regard which has been in effect for over half a century.
The last part of section 6 makes provision for appeals to the tariff board. It consolidates authority for appeal to the tariff board from decisions by the deputy minister both in respect to tariff classifications and valuation for duty, and for further appeal to the courts from the decision of the tariff board.

speechtext:
The minister has been very courteous to me in dealing with all these matters in the past. I am sure there was no discourtesy intended here; but with all respect I suggest that this house and the minister should not be put in the position of asking hon. members on this side to accept these measures without having seen them. We ought not to have to speak in this way to the government.
I want to speak briefly now on the bill itself. Its purpose is to extend the powers of what is popularly known as the Agricultural Prices Support Act, an act which is technically described as an act for the support of prices of agricultural products during the transition from war to peace.
Hon. members will recall that early in the war the government established the policy of fixing ceiling prices for agricultural products. I think it was in 1943 that we took the position, and I emphasized it time and time again, that if we were to have ceiling prices established on agricultural products to prevent prices going up at a time when they would otherwise go up, we should have a policy of establishing floor prices to prevent agricultural prices going away down in times when conditions might otherwise drive them down.
In the following year, 1944, this measure was brought in. It is in effect, as well as in name, a transitional measure, a temporary measure. That certainly was not my intention or our intention then or now. What is needed is a measure that remains in effect, not for any transitional period which the government itself may determine, but for an unfixed period as a matter of permanent policy. That is my main criticism of the bill. The bill does not provide a permanent policy.
As I have said, it is specifically set out in the title to the act that it is only for the transition period from war to peace. Mr. Speaker, the war has been over now for three years. How long is this transition period to continue? If the government is serious about having a floor price policy beyond the immediate or the near future, we should not be extending from time to time a transitional measure. It should be made a permanent policy.
With respect to the merits of this measure, the government, or members of the government, do a lot of talking about floor prices. Yet in effect, what their policy is doing is

Agricultural Prices Support Act
maintaining ceiling prices. What is the use of talking about floor prices when prices are high? They are using this and other measures not for the purpose of floor prices but for the purpose of preventing farm prices going up. They let nearly everything else go up in price, but indirectly, and in some cases directly, they are preventing farm prices from following the general trend.
This is called an Agricultural Prices Support Act. What the government is doing is keeping farm prices down, not supporting them. One does not need to go far for an illustration. The wheat board is being used for that very purpose. It was built up as a marketing institution for the benefit of producers, and it is now being used by the government, not for that purpose, but to carry a policy of government to part of the price control principle of keeping farm prices from following the normal trend under these conditions.
I have just three comments to make on the measure. The first I have referred to. It is a transitional measure and not a permanent measure. When the impression is left, as it is commonly left with the people of the country, that we have a permanent floor price policy, we are only inviting criticism, doubt and cynicism on the part of the public when we continue to deal with measures from time to time in this manner.
The second point is this. By following policies of the general character of this measure, the government has failed to lay the basis for a permanent policy to provide equitable prices for farmers in the future. They had an opportunity and they lost it. There was a time, and it is with us still, when there was a great demand for wheat, a demand which made the price much higher than it had been in the past. Instead of allowing our wheat to sell at what it was worth, the government required it to be sold at much less. Had the government allowed it to be sold at what it was worth, had they allowed the farmers to receive for it an equitable, a parity, a fair price, the balance being set aside as a reserve, that reserve would have been sufficient to supplement low prices later on for ten or twenty years.
Various figures have been suggested as to what has been lost by the wheat deal with Britain. Some put it at 8300 million in two years, and others suggest a higher amount. If we had been allowed to take the world price for this commodity, and if the farmers had been allowed to receive from that high figure a fair price for it now, the balance to be used as a measure to supplement prices when they 5849-358i
might be low later on, we could have laid a permanent basis for equitable prices for our farmers for years to come.
As it is, we have kept the price of wheat down, and because the price of wheat has been kept down, coarse grains have been down, and because coarse grains were down livestock prices were kept down indirectly. Because of such policies, we have been denied the right to sell our livestock in the United States. And that brings me to the third point.
The government is now further destroying the confidence of the public in itself and in government generally, by its action with respect to livestock. Across the line to the south the price of beef cattle is 10, 12 and 14 cents per pound higher than it is here. We are denied that market as a matter of government policy, and yet the Minister of Agriculture comes along and leaves the impression that we are going to be allowed to get into that market. He leaves the impression that the embargo is to be removed. He leaves that impression but the government takes no action; and when that impression is left what happens? The farmers hold back stock, expecting a higher price for it. I do not say that they all do, but they can do it, and it looks as if it has been done. They can hold back stock, and the price of meat goes up, and now we have the consumer facing rising meat prices because of that intimation that the embargo would be removed and that prices would go up. The consumers are facing these rising prices at home, and yet we are denied the United States market for that product.
As I said yesterday on another matter, we are getting the worst of two worlds; the embargo has not been removed and yet we have rising prices at home. I will take just a moment or two to read an extract from a western paper showing the reaction to policies of this kind. The Winnipeg Tribune of June 18 states:
Over the week end Winnipeg housewives and restaurant keepers had a hollow feeling in their stomachs as they watched the price of various cuts of beef shoot up as much as 18 cents a pound. (Naturally they were wondering why meat should suddenly jump in price at a time of year when prices usually decline.

subtopic: POWERS OF AGRICULTURAL PRICES SUPPORT BOARD EXTENDED BEYOND MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject before us is the second reading of a bill to amend the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944. It is unfortunate that this bill, which came up for first reading in April of this year, comes down to the house now alt this late date. I support the bill because it is one part of a policy to give stability to our agricultural producers; but in my opinion it is unfortunate that it is not properly integrated with other types of policies in order to provide the measure of stability that should .prevail in agriculture. In order to have a workable plan, even under this act, it is necessary to integrate that policy with a policy of stability in agriculture, namely, parity prices. In order to do that we

would have to establish a parity by which our agricultural producers would get a fair price for their products, thus giving them a decent standard of living. Having established that base parity, we would have to arrive at a formula under which, when the costs of agriculture increased in the various productive fields, we would increase the parity price so that our producers would be able to get out of their produce the money with which to buy back enough goods to preserve a proper balance with the base period. It is unfortunate that we have not used the Agricultural Prices Support Act in order to do that.
I had an order for return in the house on February 25, 1948. My question was:
1.	How much has been spent under the agriculture support act since it was passed ill 1944?
2.	For what purposes, and to wliat amount, has this act been invoked?
The answer to the first question was that only $807,618.90 has been spent, and of that amount, $75,212.23 has been spent on administration; that $109,305.18 has been spent to cover operating losses of the meat board, the dairy products board and the special products board with respect to overseas contracts for 1946-47; that $123,101.49 has been spent for price support in respect of the 1946 potato orop in the eastern provinces, and that $500,000 has been spent for price support in respect of the 1947 apple crop in Nova Scotia.
I quite agree with the expenditure of those moneys in order to try to bring some form of parity to the producers in those fields and alleviate some of the distress that was occasioned in marketing those products. But I want to bring to the attention of the government some of the submissions which have been made on behalf of agriculture in the last two years.
In 1947 the United Farmers of Canada and the Alberta Farmers' Union presented a brief to the Minister of Agriculture. (Mr. Gardiner). I may say that they speak on behalf of the agriculture groups in the country. One of the recommendations contained in that brief was that the foreword of the act we are now discussing should be changed to read, "An act for the support of the prices of agricultural products." I maintain that the act as it is now constituted does not meet the needs of agriculture. In other words it must be extended in its use in order that moneys may be used from the public treasury so that we can have parity in this country.
Yesterday we passed a resolution to ratify the international wheat agreement. That is one form of trying to get world peace-agreement so that we can have a flow of agricultural products from Canada to overseas importers or consumers. We have also passed

Agricultural Prices Support Act
the United Kingdom wheat agreement, with which I am in accord; because as a producer and as a member of the House of Commons I recognize the fact that, until we give stability to agricultural producers in this country, we cannot have any stability whatsoever in our economy at large.
Since agriculture is a basic industry, it is essential that one of the first things to do is to give to our agricultural producers the stability as a result of which they will not experience the booms and busts they have experienced in the past. I am in agreement with the recommendations of the United Farmers of Canada and the Alberta Farmers' Union with respect to their recommendations to the government that this act be extended and called: "An act for the support of the prices of agricultural products."
With regard to section 1, they recommend that it read:
This act may be cited as the Agricultural Parity Prices Act, 1944, amended 1947.
They go on further to recommend an amendment to section 3 to read as follows:
There shall be an agricultural parity prices board under the direction of the minister consisting of five members including a chairman and a vice-chairman to be appointed by the governor in council and who shall hold office during pleasure.
They recommend an amendment to section 9 of the act to read as follows:
The board shall be empowered to recommend a price change in regard to wheat to maintain a parity balance between agricultural prices and the cost of goods and services that agricultural producers must purchase or pay for. None of the consolidated revenue fund named in this act shall however 'be used for the purpose of adjusting wheat prices.
I could read all the recommendations, but since they have been tendered to the government I do not think I need do so at this time. Let me say, however, that in a further memorandum to the government in March of this year the interprovincial farmers' union council recommended to the government that a fact finding board be set up

have to guess when it will be removed, or how much of it will be removed, and we have the retail merchants asking the question: Are we going to be compelled to absorb losses amounting to thousands of dollars in order to pay for this experiment? At the same time we have the wholesale meat dealer wrestling with the question whether or not our cattle will be exported to the United States.
In all fairness, and with all sympathy for the members of the Liberal party, I hope they will go to their cabinet ministers in greater numbers and suggest that the people of Canada learn once and for all, without further nonsense, whether beef is going to be exported, so that we can finally arrive at the price the consumer will have to pay. At the same time let us know whether the excise tax is to be removed, so that we may know what we must pay for other commodities. When that is done, democracy will begin to function again and socialism will be a thing of the past.

subtopic: POWERS OF AGRICULTURAL PRICES SUPPORT BOARD EXTENDED BEYOND MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
After what the last speaker has said, I want to make it perfectly clear that in supporting this bill I do not consider that I am supporting socialism. I look upon this as a measure which is required in order to give fair play and justice to the primary producers of this country. The secondary industries in Canada, as in all countries, have always been in a position to set their prices high enough to return the cost of production plus a fair profit. The primary producers have never been in that position. They have always had to take whatever prices the trade wished to pay them, with a complete disregard for what it might have cost to produce the goods.
The Agricultural Prices Support Act was introduced in 1944, as has been stated already, as a temporary measure to assist in the transition from war to peace. From time to time various farm organizations have urged upon the government the desirability of making this a permanent measure. Strangely enough, at one time in this session I was laying emphasis on the fact that this measure should be made permanent, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) interjected that as far as he was concerned there was nothing in the measure which would indicate that it was not permanent. Apparently the government does not agree with him, however, because the government has found it necessary to bring down this amendment.
One reason why it is essential to maintain a measure of this kind in this country is the fact that for the past eight years the farmers have been accepting prices lower than they

could have obtained had it not been for certain government controls. The Minister of Agriculture pointed out that they had been taking these lower prices for eight years, and that in return they had been promised that prices would be stabilized. As a result the government has been trying to stabilize prices, and it has promised that stabilized prices will be maintained in future.
Just what do we mean by stabilized prices, and does this act go far enough in establishing a basis for prices of that kind? Subsection 2 of section 9 of the act states:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection one of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
If that is the basis on which the government is to proceed, I do not think there will be any criticism from agriculture. In other words, under this act it is the duty of the government to see that a fair relationship is maintained between the prices of agricultural products and the prices of the products of other industries. Under this act, in reality the farmers are guaranteed a parity price; but whether or not that is the interpretation the government will place upon this section in the future remains to be seen, because as yet we have not met a serious situation requiring action on the part of the government. That is so as far as the prairie farmers are concerned, though it may not be strictly true of other parts of the country, particularly those concerned with the production of potatoes and apples. But it is very necessary that parity prices be maintained in future in order that the farmers may obtain their fair share of the national income.
The main objection I have to the amendment now .before the house is that it continues the act merely as a temporary measure, subject to action by the governor in council. Thus we may have a repetition of what has happened already this year. We may not be aware of it, but we may find one day that section 9 has been taken out of operation by proclamation. We would like to see the legislation made permanent.

As the parliamentary assistant knows, last fall the prices of coarse grains were stabilized, and the farmers delivered their coarse grains at those low prices. I wish to say a few words on the purport of this bill, which is to amend the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944.
By section 12 of the act of 1944 it was provided that section 9 of the act should come into force on a date to be fixed, and remain in force for such period as might be determined by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette.
I am not enthusiastic about the type of economy that is spelled out in this act, but I am speaking on another point at the moment. Following the provisions of section 12 of the act, a proclamation dated the first day of April, 1946, brought the act into force for a period of two years. A further proclamation was authorized by order in council dated March 25, 1948. The Department of Agriculture was then advised by the Department of Justice that the order in council was ultra vires and that the act could be continued only by an act of parliament. We are now asked to pass an enabling act which confers upon the governor in council the prerogative of determining how long this act shall remain in force -and when I say "this act", I refer to section 9 of the act, which is the essence and the body of the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
It means that this type of legislation is subject to the whim and caprice of the minister and those about him, with the result that there is no certainty about the legislation as it affects prices of commodities covered by the act.
It may be objected that there was no great certainty in a competitive market, but at that time everybody was subject to a rule which is 5849-359J
as old as time, the rule of supply and demand. Under this enactment it is open to the government absolutely to ruin farmers in some sections of the country, as the dairy farmers in the eastern townships have been ruined, by precluding them from getting for butter a price which they were forced to demand by reason of the cost of labour and of feed. The result is that we have a shortage of butter, which is having a deleterious effect upon the health of the community, and is bringing about, in an agricultural and dairy country like ours, the necessity of importing this commodity from far lands.
The chairman appears to be a little uneasy. Possibly he is questioning whether I am speaking to the point, but I beg his attention and submit that we are asked today to enact legislation which covers all the points that were raised by the hon. member for Souris. We are today exactly in the position we were in when the act was first introduced into the house. It is open to us to discuss every aspect, every paragraph, every condition, every possibility which may arise under the act, because today, according to the government itself, there is no such act. The attempt further to enforce it by order in council was found by the Department of Justice to be in excess of the powers conferred by the act.
This house is asked to continue the manipulation of prices by the government. The war has been over for three years. Many specifics have been resorted to, to keep prices low, and what has been the result? Scarcity, high prices driving the people from the land into the cities, inadequate housing in the cities, and a whole series of maladies resulting from lack of equilibrium and lack of order, which necessarily follow from controls exercised by people who are not familiar with t'he aspect of life which they are attempting to control.
Added to all of that is the uncertainty of the enactment. Nobody knows what may be done at a propitious moment on the eve of an election, or in the heat of an election campaign. There is nothing to prevent the passing of an order in council which will create great inducements for any locality to support the administration.

I am amused at the confidence, shown by the parliamentary assistant, in the governor in council, who, he says, may extend it for one year or for two years, and that this decision will not be altered, when the proposed amendment reads-
-until the coming into force of this act and shall continue in force thereafter for such further period as the governor in- council may fix by proclamation.
Then there is the further provision:

In other words, if this amendment is adopted the governor in council can say when it shall come into force, when it shall go out, and how long it shall be continued. This is one of the simplest bills I have ever seen brought in to the house, and any discussion beyond the scope of it is beyond me. Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 363, to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUBSTITUTE "GOLD COMMISSIONER" FOR "COMMISSIONER", ETC.
speechtext:
In my opinion subsection 1 of section 45 of the original act as now amended by section 9 of this bill is too drastic and should have some safeguarding words added to it. It now reads:
(1)	As soon as reasonably possible after the recording of the claim the holder of the claim shall affix or cause to be affixed securely to each of the posts of the said claim a metal tag plainly marked or impressed with the recorded number and letter or letters, if any, of the claim, and in default the claim may be cancelled by the mining recorder on the application of anyone who in the opinion of the mining recorder has been misled by the lack of such tags.
(2)	The mining recorder on application shall supply the numbered tags, mentioned in subsection one, free of charge.
(3)	This section applies in respect of all claims recorded after the first day of June, nineteen hundred and forty-eight.
To a certain extent that follows the provision in the gold mining law of British Columbia, except that in British Columbia, before the claim is located, these metal tags are furnished by the mining recorder to the person about to locate the property, and the metal tags are put on from the start. However, if the minister prefers to have it done after the claim is recorded I am not going to quarrel with it; but I do say that in default of the metal tags on the posts, the claim should not be cancelled without an inquiry. Therefore I move an addition to subsection 1 of section 45, which, if adopted, would make the section read as follows:
... in default, the claim may be cancelled by the mining recorder on the application of anyone who in the opinion of the mining recorder has been misled by the lack of such tags, after a notice in writing by the mining recorder of a hearing before the mining recorder has been served on such claim holder and on said person or persons applying for cancellation. Said notice to contain the name or names of the persons applying for cancellation, alleging that they have been misled and stating how misled, and after a hearing of all of said parties before the mining recorder.
I think that is only fair, and it is in line with another paragraph of the same act under which co-owners of mineral claims are called upon to do their proportionate amount of the representation work annually. They must pay their proportionate amount of the renewal, and if one fails to do that, a hearing is held before the mining recorder and the defaulting owners are given a notice of the hearing. An opportunity is afforded them to come before the mining recorder at that hearing and state their case. I think the complaint should be known to the person complained of. He should know what the complaint is, and a complete hearing should be held before the mining recorder goes so far as to cancel the claim.

speechtext:
I have an amendment to this section, a copy of which I will send to the minister. Section 13 relates to the original Clauses of the act numbered 81, 82, and 82A. I am moving an amendment to be en tered as 82B.
82B. No entry granted' for a mineral claim shall be subject to cancellation in the discretion of the minister unless such cancellation is first recommended by the commissioner.
The preceding sections and subsections of section 13 refer to surveys. This Yukon Quartz Mining Act was enacted in 1924 in the second session that I attended in this House of Commons. Prior to that time, the mining law of Yukon in regard to quartz and lode mining was by order in council passed at Ottawa, regardless altogether of the circumstances pertaining to Yukon, methods of mining, and what was advisable or not advisable.
I drafted the act and submitted it to the miners of Yukon. As far as possible it met their requirements. I submitted it to the then minister of the interior, as he was called, the late Hon. Charles Stewart. He submitted it to his legal advisers and together we agreed on the act. Mr. Stewart piloted it through the house, and it has stood from 1924 down to this time with some more or less minor amendments down through the years.
In the act there was one section which the department was very anxious to have in. I did not approve it, but rather than hold mp the legislation or jeopardize it, I refrained from making any long fight against it. I was assured by the minister and his staff that the wide provisions of that section would newer be abused, and all through the years they have never been abused. No attempt was made to violate the provisions of that section until March of this year when there occurred what I regard as a violent abuse of the section. I will read the section to the committee:
The recorded owner of a mineral claim shall have a survey thereof made at his own expense by a duly qualified dominion land surveyor under instructions from the surveyor general within one year from the date upon which notification by the minister to do so may be sent to him.
2. Such notification shall not be given until the expiration of at least one year from the date upon which the claim was recorded.

3. If the survey is not made, and if the returns of such survey are not received and approved by the surveyor general within one year from the date of notification, the entry granted for the mineral claim shall be subject to immediate cancellation in the discretion of the minister.
There is too much discretion there to foe given to any minister. The section should not be brought into play unless there is absolute need of it, and in my opinion, knowing the situation in Yukon as I do, I do not think there is need of it today. Under the provisions of that section, this is the order that went out to the claim owners. Notices were prepared in Ottawa and sent to the various mining recorders of the territory:
Upon instructions from the Minister of Mines and Resources and pursuant to section 78 of the Quartz Mining Act, you are hereby notified that you must within one year from the date upon which notification is sent to you, at your own expense, have a survey made of all mineral claims owned by you which were recorded prior to March 31, 1947.
A storm of protest against that came in to the department. Then along came another letter from the mining recorder, also prepared in Ottawa and sent out to have the name put in and be sent out by the mining recorder. This is the way this demand No. 2 reads:
The increasing interest displayed in mineral resources of Yukon Territory has emphasized the necessity of having surveys made to determine the boundaries of older quartz mining claims. Many complaints have been received recently as a result of those entering the field being unable to accurately locate claims from stakes on the ground or from descriptions in the record book.
The minister has therefore authorized the enforcement of section 78, Yukon Quartz Mining Act, and I have been instructed by the minister to notify you in his behalf, and you are hereby so notified, that you shall have a survey made at your own expense by a duly qualified dominion land surveyor under instructions from the surveyor general within one year from the date of this notice, of all claims standing in your name and recorded for over one year.
Then the attention of the claimant is called to the penalty, which is that the claim shall be subject to immediate cancellation at the discretion of the minister. Then along comes another letter. The two I have read were by no means well received. No. 3 reads as fellows:
The correspondence which has been received as a result of the notices sent to claim holders under section 78 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act has been reported to the department and I have been instructed to furnish further information to all those to whom these notices have been sent, supplementing the information already given,
The necessity of a survey of mineral claims has been a fundamental requirement of the Quartz Mining Act from the beginning.

Yukon Quartz Mining Act
That is absolutely incorrect and not so.
The two-post staking system which is in effect in Yukon territory contemplates that there will be an early survey so that the boundary of each claim may be defined.
That is not a correct interpretation at all. It was never the intention that there would be an early survey. The two-post system is in effect and has been used in British Columbia for the last fifty years; and quartz mining in British Columbia is greater in magnitude than anything that has been undertaken in Yukon to date, although it is coming on. The two-post system has been satisfactory to the miners all down through the years and there has never been a demand for a change. The letter continues:
This requirement was not enforced during the time when it was imposible to obtain the services of a surveyor. The net result of this leniency-
Listen to that-"leniency".
-has been that those who wish to proceed with the development of the mineral resources of the territory are unable to ascertain the limits of the properties that can be secured either by purchase or staking.
I doubt that. If there are people of that sort who are delayed and prevented, they should come out from under cover, say who they are, say who is delaying them, and have those people who are delaying them disciplined and made subject to the provisions of this act. Do not hit the whole mining population over the head with that section. The letter continues:
Now that the services of dominion land surveyors are available it has been considered appropriate to require claim holders to have their claims surveyed. There is no intention of taking arbitrary action.
Oh, none at all.
If it is impossible to have a survey made, either because the surveyor cannot get around to it, or for good and sufficient reason the claim owner while developing the property is unable to pay the expense of the survey, then the circumstances will be considered by the minister on the representations of the claim holder.
And so on. That, I think, was the third demand.

speechtext:
Then following
those notices came a demand to the claim owners for a deposit from them of $200 per claim. A man owning ten claims had to put up $2,000. That demand was not welcomed either. Now the department has come down to $100. That is the last demand.
Further than that, there are three mining districts in Yukon; the Dawson district, the Whitehorse district and the Mayo district. I am informed by the minister's officials that no surveys are to be required in the Dawson or Whitehorse districts, but that it will all be confined to the Mayo district. That is where the big silver mines are. That is where certain people, I think, want to get more property instead of going out in a manly way and going after it. Those operators of silver-lead mines in Yukon are in the way of making millions of dollars of profit on Canadian investment, and I am glad they are. They have silver-lead ore so rich that it is hard to realize it. It is so valuable that it does not need to be milled, but only to be sorted and sent out to the smelters in its native state. To say that the people wishing to acquire claims to more property cannot find the boundaries of claims already located and that have become the property of various owners, is not correct. There is a map of all the surveyed claims in that silver mining area and there is a blueprint in the mining recorder's office at Mayo and Dawson, showing the location not only of the surveyed claims but of all the recorded claims.
If people are anxious to acquire a property from claim owners, those claim owners will go out and show them where the boundaries are and what they have to acquire. I have received-as I am sure the minister and his staff have also-literally hundreds of protests. I have one protest here containing signatures of over 164 claim owners against that attempt on the part of the minister's officials to drive those claim owners into having their claims surveyed. The minister will pardon me if I quote from a letter written to me by him, dated May 25. He says:
It may interest you to know that in the Northwest Territories the department employs mining inspectors to see that the assessment work which is claimed by affidavit is actually performed on the claims. So far, this has not been the policy undler the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. You are aware, of course, that the British Columbia mining administration, which has two-post staking, employes mining inspectors.
I can understand that the minister is not up to date on the policy of his department, because he has only come to it. But he saya that it has not been the policy under the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. When this quartz mining act was passed in 1924, mining inspectors were at once appointed; they did their work, inspected the claims and saw that the mining was done properly and with safety to the miners in the mine. But for some unaccountable reason the government and the department have dropped the position of
Yukon Quartz Mining Act

mining inspector altogether and we have no mining inspectors in Yukon. That is not the fault of the miners; it is the fault of the government itself. When the minister says it is not the policy, it is true it is not the policy, but it is provided by the act. British Columbia has the two-post staking system and its mining inspectors. We should have our mining inspectors, and we want the staking in Yukon to be the twonpost staking. I set out the situation fully in a letter I wrote the minister; and with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should' like to read that letter and have it on record, because to the miners of Yukon this is a most important matter. On May 20 I wrote the then acting minister, whose appointment I am glad to say has been confirmed, saying:
The Yukon Quartz Mining Act was enacted by the parliament of Canada in 1924.
In the 24 years the act has been in operation mineral claims have been located, owned, sold and mined with entire satisfaction to both companies and individuals owning them, and until March of this year, no minister of mines, nor any of his staff has abused the power given the minister by section 78 of the act by notifying the recorded owners of unsurveyed' mineral claims in Yukon that a survey of the claims must be made at their expense by a fully qualified dominion land surveyor under instructions from the surveyor general within one year from the date upon which such notification by the minister to do so may be sent to him, and if the survey is not made, and if the returns of such survey are not received and approved by the surveyor general within one year from the date of notification, the entry granted for the mineral claim shall be subject to immediate cancellation in the discretion of the minister.
I need not read the whole letter, but in it I set out the various notices I have already read to the committee. Then I said to the minister, as I now say to the committee:
The department of mines states there are in Yukon approximately 1,057 recorded unsurveyed mineral claims, and it is assigning a surveyor to make surveys of mineral claims in Yukon, that such surveying in Yukon can he done during three or four months of the year, depending on locality. It follows that it will take a number of years to have those claims surveyed.
At the time this letter was written the amount demanded of the claim owners was $200 a claim, and I was acting on that figure. As I have already said, it has been reduced to $100 a claim.
Two hundred dollars per claim is exacted from the owners of the 1,657 unsurveyed claims. That will be $331,460-
Now, at S100 a claim, it will be half that amount, but these words will apply to that figure just as they applied to the earlier figure. -which sum or any part of it, if expended in prospecting and development work would do far more to develop mining than if tied up for unnecessary surveys.

As to the two-post system, the predecessors of the mining companies operating there now produced in a few years from those few mines values in silver-lead of over $25,000,000. The amendment I have moved provides that no entry granted for a mineral claim shall be subject to cancellation in the discretion of the minister unless such cancellation is on the recommendation of the commissioner. With all respect to the minister, he must remember that he is not a miner. He is here in Ottawa, three or four thousand miles from the mines to which this law is to apply. He has a perfectly good commissioner who, before being appointed to that position, was a lawyer practising first in Winnipeg and later in the mining camp of Yellowknife. He is in sympathy with the miners; he knows what they need, and he would never recommend the cancellation of a mining claim unless there was great misbehaviour on the part of the owner.
I ask the minister: Why penalize the owners of all claims, in even one of the three mining districts, if there are people holding unsurveyed mineral claims and who, as a result, are hampering progress and preventing other claims from being acquired? Let those who are complaining come into the open and say who is holding them up. Then the minister and his officials can quickly attend to those people and make them get out of the way. But do not make this apply to all the law-abiding miners in the whole Mayo district.
Therefore I considered it necessary and advisable to offer the amendment, and I only hope the minister will see his way clear to permit it to go through.

I did not attempt to interrupt the hon. member while he was commenting on section 78 of the act, which is not being amended at all by this bill. This matter, with respect to which the hon. member for Yukon read certain instructions that were sent out by the department, has been the subject of conversations between my officials and myself and others interested, including the hon. member for Yukon. Following those discussions, new instructions were issued, which I believe meet with the approval of the hon. member. That is why I was anxious to have him read the full statement, to show that the clauses to which he objected have already been amended by the department.
I could go into the various points raised, but I do not think it is necessary. There was a real demand from people interested in mining development for the surveying of various claims in the Yukon territory. It is the intention of the department only to survey those claims alongside present developments, in order to

Yukon Quartz Mining Act
enable the men doing development work, as well as those in close proximity to those properties, to know exactly the extent of the claims.
We are following the two-post staking in the Yukon; that has always been followed there and in British Columbia. Each claim holder is required to do S100 worth of work on his development each year in order to hold the claim. The department is providing a surveyor to survey any claims that require to be ' surveyed, and we are doing that work for S100. That will be accepted as a discharge in full of the necessary work on the claim for that year.
I am sorry I cannot accept the amendment to section 13 by adding, as the hon. member suggests, a provision that no entry granted for a mineral claim shall be subject to cancellation in the discretion of the minister unless such cancellation is first recommended by the commissioner. There is no doubt in the world that, before the minister ever acts, he gets advice from the commissioner, and on that advice he takes action. I think it would be a retrograde step for the minister here at Ottawa to attempt to throw off any of his own responsibility in a matter of this kind. I believe the minister must accept and assume the final responsibility; and the information upon which he acts is the information and the recommendation coming from the commissioner. Under those circumstances I do not see how' I can accept this amendment.

speechtext:
WTould the minister advise the committee if there is anything in the regulations making it imperative that the minister should have a report from the commissioner before acting? I agree with the minister that responsibility rests with the minister. He should exercise it and assume all the praise or penalties that might arise from the decision at which he arrives. If I am correctly informed, mining is not only an important industry in the Yukon territory, it is possibly, the only one.
In the last few months something has come about that has caused a great deal of anxiety among the hardy breed of men called miners or prospectors. It would seem unfortunate if anything should occur w'hich would tend to diminish their enthusiasm or energy in the pursuit of their difficult and burdensome calling. The minister has not said that new' conditions have not come into existence. I did not understand from the hon. member for Yukon exactly what had aroused the fears, if not the suspicions of his constituents, but apparently about March last a number of threats of cancellation or cancellations took place.
Would there be any particular difficulty in inserting in the regulations a provision whereby an action taken by the minister should be preceded by a report from the commissioner?
I am not suggesting that the minister be bound by that report because, as he has well said, the responsibility is his, and I for one am content that it should remain where it belongs in its entirety, upon the shoulders of the minister. But, after all, the minister is far away from the Yukon. The Yukon is now more accessible in some ways than it has ever been before, and it is possible that practices which formerly did not obtain in that country may be germinating there and causing hardship to the prospectors and miners. It seems to me that if that provision were in the regulations the minister would get a report which W'ould be based upon the facts, and among those facts would be the views of the prospector or owner of the claim. Therefore no hurried decision would be taken, and I think the situation would be met.
Apparently there is something new', because for twenty-four years this act has been administered, as I understand, to the entire satisfaction of the population of the Yukon. But today that population is disturbed and upset. There must be some reason for that. I am sure that the minister wishes the important work of prospecting to go on and that those who follow that calling should have all the protection that good administration will provide. Therefore I ask him if he does not consider it feasible to put into the regulations that provision which would lead these people to believe that they will continue to receive the equitable administration which they have known in the past.

It will be a pleasure to do so, as requested by the minister. This editorial appeared in the Western Miner, published at Vancouver, and is dated June 1948. It reads:
The Department of Mines and Resources would be well advised to reconsider its present attitude regarding compulsory surveying of mineral claims in Yukon teirritory. A bureaucratic interpretation of section 78 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act now provides that owners of mineral claims in Yukon must, within one year, have their claims surveyed by a dominion land surveyor and have the survey approved by the surveyor general. Failing this, entries granted for such Claims will be subject to immediate cancellation in the discretion of the Minister of Mines. Seeking to defend its position, the government states that: "The necessity of a survey of mineral claims1 has been a fundamental requirement of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act from the beginning. The two-post staking system which is in effect in the Yukon territory contemplates that there will be an early survey so that the boundary of each claim may be defined. This requirement \vas not enforced during the time when it was impossible to obtain the services of a surveyor. The net result of this leniency has been that those who wish to proceed with the development of the mineral resources of the territory are unable to ascertain the limits of the properties that can be secured either by purchase or staking"-and (2) "Now that the services of dominion land surveyors are available, it has been considered appropriate to require claim holders to have their claims surveyed. There is no intention of taking arbitrary action. If it is impossible to have a survey made, either because the surveyor cannot get around to it, or for good and sufficient reason the claim owner, while developing his property, is unable to pay the expense of the survey, then the circumstances will be considered by the minister on the representations of the claim holder." All of which is a fine-sounding hit of official gobbledygook and nothing more.
It is interesting to note that George Black, M.P., long associated with Yukon mining, states definitely that when the Quartz Mining Act was drafted and when it was submitted to parliament in 1924 there was absolutely no contemplation, under the two-post staking system, of an early survey. Certainly the member for Yrukon, who drafted the original legislation, is more competent to pass on the intent of parliament than tlhe civil servants who are now trying to impose their own interpretation. Aside from that point, altogether, it is difficult to understand why the department should try to hang this question of surveys on such a tenuous thread as the two-post staking method. And to advance the argument that surveys are necessary because those who wish to proceed with the development of the mineral resources of the territory are unable to

Yukon Quartz Mining Act
ascertain limits of properties, is nothing short of crass stupidity. To date surveys have not been found necessary in other parts of Canada when mining claims change hands, .and if the four-post staking method provides the answer, why not have any claims in question restaked using four posts? Surely it is not the desire of the department to impose on prospectors a penalty of $200 per claim held in Yukon territory to overcome a deficiency in staking regulations which have been in force for almost a quarter of a century. In actual fact, of course, once the government's base linos have been run, any company engineer could readily "ascertain the limits" of the claims in question, and if they warrant development such a survey would be made as a matter of course.
To state that the government was "lenient" in not enforcing the survey regulations during the time when it was impossible to obtain the services of a surveyor is patently bureaucratic balderdash and is repeated here only as a further example of official circumlocution. The same applies to item (2) in the government statement. Just what do they mean when they say there is no intention to take arbitrary action? If the question of whether or not a prospector holds title to a claim rests with the idiosyncracies of the surveyor who may or may not "get around to it", or with the personal whim of the minister and his subordinates, depending on whether or not the department happens again to feel in a "lenient" mood, there will be little or no new mining development in Yukon territory.
As everyone associated with mining knows, the future of the industry in this country rests on the discovery and development of new deposits. It is the prospector who stakes the original claims and does the preliminary development. His position is one of paramount importance and every possible assistance and encouragement must be rendered him if we are to offset the rapid depletion of known ore bodies. These are fundamentals which one would expect even the Ottawa desk miners to recognize. Instead of suggesting that the department bear the cost of any claim surveys deemed essential to the further development of mineral resources, however, (and the amount involved would be inconsequential) the best that has been forthcoming to date is that the prospectors. by way of encouragement no doubt, Should hand over $200 per claim or face the probability of cancellation. Apart from the fact that most prospectors don't have that kind of money, if they did have $200 per claim to spend one would think that the greatest possible benefit to all concerned would come from spending it on additional development. Nobody in his right mind wants to have a mineral claim surveyed at a cost of $200 until he is reasonably assured that he stands a chance of getting his money back some day. And particularly in these times when it is all too difficult to interest venture capital in mine development (thanks in great part to Ottawa's long-haired idealists), prospectors are having a tough time just getting by, without any additional burdens. If the department really wants to help the Yukon prospectors in their efforts to find and develop new mines, the compulsory survey regulations should be deleted from the quartz mining act immediately. Otherwise the Yukon prospectors say they will quit the territory, and they mean it.
I apologize to my fellow members for being for once a bit long-winded, but I tried, to avoid it.
