speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was sworn in as Minister of Mines and Resources on June 11, eleven days ago. I am not on that account asking for any compassion, although I am very much appreciative-

That is a good item to start
with.

Supply-Mines and Resources

I have been in close touch in many ways and for many years with the Department of Mines and Resources, the old department of the interior, but from the other side of the desk. My first experience with the department was back in the early days when I was an employee of the then minister of the interior, the Hon. Frank Oliver, publisher of the Edmonton Bulletin.
I think everybody admits that he was one of Canada's great statesmen.
I should like to give a brief summary of the estimates of the department before we proceed with the individual items. The estimates of the Department of Mines and Resources provide for a considerable increase -$12,150,000-over those of the previous year. In large measure this increase reflects a situation which has been accumulating for a number of years. During the depression and war years, expenditures for improvements in the national parks and Indian reserves and for the development of the Northwest Territories and Yukon were, of necessity greatly curtailed. The result has been that the ordinary facilities in the parks and Indian reserves have so deteriorated that larger appropriations are now required to meet the most urgent needs. We are under most severe pressure from the Northwest Territories and Yukon where we have nearly twenty years of arrears to make up. Normal development of these areas cannot be longer delayed.
With the cessation of hostilities and the resulting increase in available manpower, the mining industry is stepping up its activity and making more requests for mineral dressing investigations. Also, reconversion problems and post-war increase in industrial activity have resulted in man}' demands for physical metallurgy investigations.
A new laboratory will shortly be completed and equipped with semi-commercial sized rolling mill, extrusion press and other equipment primarily for work on light metals and their alloys. Operation of this laboratory will account for a considerable part of the additional appropriation now asked for.
Similarly, with the forest industry, post-war demands for investigation and research in silviculture, fire prevention and forest management have greatly expanded, and this is reflected in this increase in the estimates. There has been a much larger use of timber in recent years, first to meet the needs of war, and subsequently the demands of peacetime requirements. For many years our industries dependent on the forest for their raw material were able to cut out, and move on to areas of new supplies. There is a limit to the distance
that industries can go for supplies, and more industrialists are now giving thought to a policy of forest management to continue production on accessible forest lands.
It will be seen that a large part of the increase in our estimates is to provide funds for the operations of the eastern Rockies forest conservation board, a joint dominion-provincial organization created by statute last year to plan, direct and supervise the construction, operation and maintenance of all projects and facilities required for the proper protection and conservation of the forests and the protection of the watersheds within the area of the eastern Rockies.
The demand for accurate maps for the development of Canada's natural resources, particularly of northern Canada, is reflected in the increase in the appropriations requested for the surveys and mapping units of the department, which include also the charting of our shores. It is intended this year to provide two new hydrographic ships for this purpose.
If Canada hopes to attract United States tourists, it will be necessary to appropriate sufficient funds to ensure that present facilities in our national parks are attractive and adequate and that improvements are made where required. It is particularly important that facilities be made available for the man in the average income bracket. Therefore an active parks program must be initiated at once. A new road development program for the parks is planned, which will include the reconstruction and preparation for hard-surfacing of roads which are inferior in quality and the improvement of hazardous portions of existing roads. A modest building program will also be undertaken.
The government of New Brunswick recently transferred to the dominion an area of land for the creation of a n_tional park, and it is proposed to make a start on the new park this year.
As mentioned before, during the depression and war years expenditures for buildings and other construction projects in the Indian reserves were so curtailed that not only is it necessary now to ask for substantial increases for the repairs to Indian buildings and houses, but the accumulation of new building needs has reached the stage where it is not possible to carry on the administration of Indian affairs without considerably increased appropriations for building purposes.
A substantial increase is required for Indian education. It is proposed next year to provide ninety-seven new classrooms for day school purposes and four residential schools in isolated
Supply-Mines and Resources

locations. There are 12,000 Indian children of school age for whom no educational facilities have yet been provided. We can make some progress with the adult Indian, but the education of the child is where the work must begin if the Indian is to become a useful citizen. 'His health, habits, energies and ambitions must be supervised and directed, and this can best be done through the school, where early and continuous training will fit him to take his place in the life of the country. This cannot be accomplished without modern, clean, well-lighted school buildings and qualified teachers.
A large part of the increase in the vote for Indian welfare is necessary for the construction of Indian houses. In most cases the Indians build their own houses from material supplied, in many instances the lumber being from their own sawmills. In this way the greatest number of houses is secured with the minimum expenditure of funds.
It is necessary to ask for a considerable increase for immigration purposes also. This is due largely to the necessity of providing adequate facilities both in Canada and abroad to deal with the increasing flow of immigrants and visitors to this country.

I do not want to say anything that will bother the minister, because I know he has been only a short time in this department, and I know his whole heart is in the development of this country, particularly the western country and the far north. But there are three general programs I should like to ask a word about, and if the minister cannot answer, that will be all right.
In former years there was always an item in these estimates for proceeding with the work of development of oil from the tar sands at Fort McMurray. I do not see anything in the estimates for that purpose this year; yet I know that this country has an investment there in cash of approximately $2,000,000 in one way or another. If the minister knows,
I would ask him just what the position is at Fort McMurray today. The main separation plant was burnt down. I saw it after it was burnt. I may be going there again this year, but I am not sure that I shall have time to go. Can the minister tell the committee just the situation of the buildings there which belong to the government and whether any equipment is still there? If he cannot answer that, I have two other questions to ask.

There will be a substantial item in the supplementaries to provide for further research work in connection with the development of the so-called tar sands at Fort McMurray. All the plant and equipment

that we had at Waterways has been sold to the Abasand company. They are maintaining the buildings and the refinery.

Have they rebuilt the
separation plant?
No.

The refinery, then, is just standing where it was before, at the rear of where the separation plant was located? Is all the equipment under protection? The new Abasand company, an Edmonton company, is under the direction, I believe, of the Alberta government.
This is entirely separate from the development down the Athabaska river, which is being assisted by the Alberta government.

I do not think I shall worry the minister any more, because I can see he is not familiar with the matter.
I observe an item in the estimates for coal development in the Yukon area, and I am glad to see that item. My hon. friend the member for Yukon is familiar with the Yukon's resources, and I am very glad we have coal in the Yukon. Part of the business of the Department of Mines and Resources should be the development of coal anywhere. Is the minister conversant with the probable development of hard coal in the Highwood area of Alberta?

I am familiar in a general way with the coal resources of the Highwood area and other high-grade coal resources in other parts of the eastern slope of the Rockies. I do not know just what information my hon. friend seeks. But he did refer to the development of coal properties in the Yukon.	Moneys have been
advanced to assist in the opening up of coal deposits there to serve the Yukon on a basis on which the government hopes to be reimbursed through sales.

The minister is new in the department. I hope he will be better by next year. The minister will be more familiar with what the department is doing with reference to oil, if it comes under his department. Will he tell us how much oil has been delivered in the Leduc area so far and what the prospects are?

I should like to give what answer I can to the hon. member. The so-called Leduc sector of the Edmonton oil field is, as everyone knows, under great development at the present time. Unfortunately, the work there has recently been held

Supply-Mines and Resources
up by a very large producer getting out of control. That difficulty has not yet been fully overcome.
They got it under control the day before yesterday.

The hon. member for Calgary West must have later information on that than I have. On my last inquiry I was informed that, although they were making great progress in getting the well under control, they had not yet succeeded. I am delighted to know that the well is now under control.
The last newspaper from the west carried that information.
I am sorry, but I cannot give the figures of the amount of oil produced there. The amounts vary from day to day.

I was pleased! to hear the minister say that his department was taking an interest in putting better roads in our national parks. Of course roads in the west are a major problem. The great trouble is that you maj' have good roads in the parks, but in the process of getting to the parks you wreck your car. I notice in the votes that money is allocated for road construction into the Northwest Territories, and into the Yellowknife district.
Within my own riding <we have an area called Atlin, in which placer mining is carried on to a considerable extent. I do not want to ride the. Department of Mines and Resources, because I do not believe they are wholly to blame for what happened. It might be this unknown quantity called the treasury board. British Columbia offered to pay their share of the road amounting to $100,000 from Atlin up to the Yukon border if the federal authority would pay their $100,000 and build their half of the road from the British Columbia border to the Alcan highway. This investment of $200,000 would have produced almost as large an amount as that. It would have paid for itself in the actual value of gold produced. On top of that you could liken it to a park area, because perhaps it is the most beautiful townsite in Canada. At Atlin lake there is fishing and hunting for big game. It is my understanding that, although the government of British Columbia offered to pay its $100,000, the federal government would not come through with its half. It would have been an acquisition to the country. It would have been an attraction to the tourists and would have side-tracked many who go to Fairbanks. They would have turned down and gone to Atlin. I should like the department to keep that in
mind when making up next year's estimates, because it is impossible to develop that placer mining field unless roads are put in. They cannot get the heavy equipment in until the road is built.

I am happy that we have the minister as head of this department. I was glad to hear what he had to say in regard to the government taking action on conservation of our forests and investigation into our mineral resources and how to use them. If wre had had proper conservation of our forests in the past twenty-five years we would not have had the terrific forest fires which I myself saw in flying over the Chapleau area of northern Ontario. It is to be regretted that, owing to policies followed in Canada under which timber operators were given large timber berths and allowed to cut the timber and leave slashings in the forests, huge fires have resulted. The department has been unable to prevent terrible losses, amounting to millions of dollars, in our timber berths. I hope that the minister will take measures to guard against further fires of that kind.
Another matter to which I should like to refer is that of our various mineral deposits. I want to refer particularly to the potash deposits in Saskatchewan. I am told by authorities of the federal government that these deposits are of extreme importance; and, should we exploit them properly, they will perhaps be of as great significance as the potash deposits in Germany. Indeed they offer as great an opportunity for potash development as we find in some of the fields in Mexico. If the minister has any information on that I should like him to pass it on to us. Will he give us any communications or plans of development of the potash deposits that have passed between the federal government and the government of Saskatchewan? I think he will readily recognize that it is a tremendous proposition. It would take sums of money running into many millions of dollars properly to develop that field. If we had a progressive attitude toward that development we could have a large export surplus of potash to send to other countries, and this would assist us to correct our unfavourable balance of trade with other nations.

There has been correspondence between the department and the government of Saskatchewan regarding the development of potash resources, but no decision has been arrived at. In connection with the forests, it is the intention of the department to bring in, at the next session, a forests act which will look toward the development and preservation of our timber resources.
Supply-Mines and Resources

Will the minister not make a statement in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Skeena? It is of the utmost importance that a road should be constructed between the Atlin country and the Alaska highway. Apparently the provin-nial government has offered to pay half the cost. What position is being taken by the dominion government?

I do not want to block my own estimates. I was quite ready to answer the question of the hon. member for Skeena by informing him that the item of which he spoke-and of which he spoke as being a matter that was lost for this session- is still under consideration. I am not sure what the result will be. Instead of being a cost of $100,000 to the provincial government and $100,000 to the dominion government, it is expected by our officials that the cost will be at least double that to both the province and the federal government. But the need is recognized. The wealth of the mineral field that this road will open up is recognized. Everything cannot be done at once. We are building roads in the Yukon territory alone this year to the extent of $425,000.

I should like to ask the minister a question. I understand that he is a new minister and I am a new member, so that we start on a fairly even level, although possibly he will have the advantage. I should like to inquire especially about the policy of this department in regard to Indians who are over the age of seventy. In British Columbia there are a number of Indians living in reservations on the borders of the constituency I represent, and I understand from them-I should like to check this with the minister-that recently this department has granted an increase of $8 a month to these aged people. Previously they were receiving something in the nature of $5 a month, which was given them in the form of necessities by the Indian agent. The condition of these people at the present time is most necessitous. We are all aware that anyone of the white race who is asked to live on $40 a month as an old age pension is in no paradise; and when we consider that these Indian races eat as we eat and have to live as we have to live, what they receive is a remarkably small sum. Does the department intend to increase the amount? When I say "increase," I do not mean increasing it another $8, but increasing it in line with the cost of living.

Item agreed to.
Mines, forests and scientific services branch- Bureau of mines-[DOT]
18i. Mineral resources investigations, $1,135,857.
Will the minister explain the work carried out under this vote?

The apparent increase is $512,723. However, in 1947-48 there was provided in votes 532 and 534 of the demobilization and reconversion estimates the sum of $384,500 for services being carried on in the divisions of mineral dressing and metallurgy and mineral resources. This will be continued in 1948-49 under, the main vote. The difference between this amount and the apparent increase of $512,723 represents an actual increase of $128,223. The vote provides for office, laboratory and field investigations relating to metallic minerals, industrial minerals, fuels and mineral economics, including those directly connected with post-war problems, and the laboratories equipped to carry out investigations on both small and semi-commercial scales are housed in several modern buildings on Booth street, Ottawa. Investment in buildings and equipment is almost $3,000,000. As a group, these laboratories are probably without their equal anywhere. The services provided are in ever-increasing demand by industry and by other government agencies.
The help is available to all the provinces and not merely to the Northwest Territories?
It is for all Canada.

I wish to congratulate the minister on this increase in the estimates of the department, and I would ask him whether these laboratories are being extended in any considerable degree. To what extent will the increase be available for increase in the metallurgical staff dealing with these problems? It is well known in the mining industry that there has been great delay in getting results, and with this increase we hope that the service can be brought up to date.

Supply-Mines and Resources
The staff is being constantly increased. We have just finished equipping a new laboratory and are planning the erection of two additional buildings at an approximate cost of $35,000.
There is an increase of only four in the permanent staff. That is what I had in mind. There should be a greater increase in the technical personnel of the department.
While there is an increase of only four in the permanent staff, there is a large increase in the temporary staff.

The minister says there is a large increase in the temporary staff, but in spite of the increase in wages over last year there is an increase of only $2,000 for temporary staff. It seems to me you are spending a great deal of money but not filling up the staff to do the job you propose to do.

When these expenditures are made for investigation into mineral resources in any province, are they made on a proportionate basis with the province concerned? When you go into a province to investigate certain mineral resources, does the department spend dollar for dollar with the province?
There is no formula that is used in all cases. It is a matter of arriving at an arrangement in accordance with the necessities of development.

Will the minister state whether he will increase the personnel of that branch above $2,000 for temporary assistance so as to give better service to industry?
'Mr. MacKINNON: From what I learn from my officials, there is a much larger increase than would be indicated by the $2,000 mentioned, and the staff is, I am told, being increased.

Item agreed to.
Mines, forests and scientific services branch'- Bureau of mines-
160.	Investigations of radioactive ores, $134,200.

This vote calls for
$134,000 odd. This particular branch does not seem to have any head. Most of the expenses are connected with temporary staff in the amount of $78,000 out of $134,000. Much of the rest is for travelling expenses and supplies. Just what are they doing and where are they finding the material, if that can be stated?

I am informed that this is a subject in respect of which, inasmuch as it deals with radioactive ores, the department is
careful in the information it makes public. I can say, however, that the project has been underway since 1945 and was undertaken at the request of the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the president of the national research council. At the outset the objective was to improve the recovery of pitchblende from the ore of the crown company, Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, but this has since been expanded to include ores from other sources. The investigation is part of a much larger and highly secret project on atomic energy which is being carried out by certain government departments.

I thought it had reference to other ores, because the country owns the whole area at Great Bear lake and, I presume, all the properties roundabout. I can quite realize that the department does not want to reveal where they are, and I will not press the question if they do not wish to. I was wondering where those other areas are in which the investigators are trying to discover radioactive ores.
It is nearly all research work done here in Ottawa.
That is apart from Eldorado Mines, I take it?
Yes.
Can the minister tell us how many investigations for the last year are covered by that item? The vote is for $134,000. How many separate analyses were made of radioactive ores in the last year?
I am afraid I cannot give that information.
Is that work done for the atomic energy control board?
Yes, and for Chalk River.

Item agreed to.
Mines, forests and scientific services branch- Dominion forest services-
168. Forest research and investigations, $649,639.

I was pleased to hear the minister say a few minutes ago that the government planned a forest act next year. Will he outline to the committee what this forest act will embrace or what sort of thing is being contemplated by the government?

The details of the contemplated forest act have not yet beeh worked out, but it is planned to assist the forest industry throughout Canada.
Supply-Mines and Resources
May I ask if the minister plans to call a conference with the forestry branches of the provincial governments before passing this act, in order to find out how the federal government can help them?

It has been my good fortune in another department to work closely on matters of mutual interest to the provinces and the dominion. I am quite sure that this problem will be approached on the same basis.

May I just tell the minister what I have been trying to get at in the last two questions? It is simply this. The provinces obviously need help in fire prevention. The federal government holds within its hands the greatest weapon by means of which to protect the provinces against forest fires; I refer to the Royal Canadian Air Force. The minister's department has already been able to work ably and well with the R.C.A.F. in the mapping project. In regard to forest conservation and protection from fires, the minister's department should undertake, with the provinces of Canada, a regular plan of action and scheme to put a force of machines to work, and not just one, as they have at the present time in northern Ontario. They should put a whole force of machines into action, with dry ice and every other form of fire-fighting equipment, so that we can conserve our natural wealth. In that way our armed forces at the same time will be doing the country a great service.

I am happy to hear what the hon. member for Trinity lias just, said, coming as I do from a province in which we have given great consideration to the losses in our forests and in which we have undertaken to train young men to jump by parachute from planes in order to stop forest fires in their early stages. This has meant that we in Saskatchewan feel that if we can get co-operation from the federal government in this regard, we shall go a long way in inducing the menace of fires and the destruction of our valuable timber.
I should like to ask the minister with regard to this item 168-which is for the substantial amount of 8640,000, an increase of 84)1,000 over last year-if it is the policy of the government to investigate the by-products of our timber. in Saskatchewan we now have research going on to utilize a great deal of our timber which formerly went to waste in the form of slabs and portions of our trees which could not be used for lumber. I should like the minister to give us at some length, if he would be so kind, information in that regard.

This involves specialized studies including the following:
Silvicultural investigations concerning the growth of different tree species, natural regeneration, and methods to improve forest stands peculiar to the various forest regions of Canada; to determine the factors affecting the forest growth, reproduction and depletion in all its phases and to evolve from such studies basic data for improved forest management on areas accessible for exploitation.
To determine the forest inventory of Canada with relation to its accessibility for marketing, the volume of merchantable timber available to industry and the relationship between production and depletion, so that industry can be geared to the growth potential of the forest.
To develop scientific methods to expedite the collection of forest inventory data through technique and scientific devices to interpret forestry data from air photographs.
The study of factors of tariffs, taxation, et cetera, on sale of forest products in world markets as they affect both the internal and external economy of Canada.
And finally, to determine and correlate the factors involved in measuring forest fire danger, including temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind velocity and evaporation, as they affect the inflammability of the various forest fuels; the design, testing and development of equipment and methods to increase the efficiency of forest fire detection and suppression.

Will the minister tell us how much money he has at his disposal for expenditure in the matter of detecting and fighting forest fires? It is one thing to have a beautiful plan laid out for the next twenty-five years; and it is another thing to have something with which to stop a forest fire next week, if it breaks out in Ontario or British Columbia or Albert and destroys more forests than all our highfalutin ideas on reforestation would replace in 100 years. We w'ant to know what we are to have done right away. How much money has the minister available to spend?
More forest fires are put out by rain than by anything else.

Apart from the protection of our forests in our national parks, in the Yukon, Northwest Territories and experimental stations, forest fire protection is a matter purely for the provinces.

Supply-Mines and Resources

I will grant that,
according to the British North America Act, it is a responsibility of the provinces, but it should be borne in the mind of every member of the government of Canada that every stick of timber that is destroyed in any province is a loss to Canada. We can just figure out the responsibility of the government in the light of that fact. I suppose it is too late for the minister to bring any influence to bear upon the government this year, but I would suggest that for next year he request that a liberal allowance be granted with which to co-operate in putting out fires which may occur at any time in any province of Canada.

Item agreed to.
Mines, forests and scientific services branch- Dominion forest service-
169. Forest products research, $435,862.

This item deals with
forest products research, which is a matter of deep interest to many people living in British Columbia, where the forest industry is of such importance. It is of particular interest also to many people I have the honour to represent. I should like the minister to give us some information in detail as to the type of research being carried on in connection with forest products, the staff engaged in that program in British Columbia at the present time, and the projects on which they are working. Again, I should like to know how this information is given to the operators of forest industries and others concerned. I speak with some knowledge of the forest industry in my own constituency, since I have been engaged in it to a certain extent for nearly forty years. From my experience I can say we have a tremendous waste in forest products even today. For instance, if it were not for the expensive equipment required we could make from sawdust excellent briquettes which burn satisfactorily, but at the present time all these processes are far too expensive to be used by small mills. I could go on almost endlessly mentioning the things in which we are interested as far as forest products research is concerned, but I should like the minister to give us some idea of the projects being undertaken at this time, and particularly the work being done in British Columbia.

This vote provides for the operation of the forest products laboratories, which are in three units: first, the Ottawa laboratory, concerned with research and studies primarily affecting the sawmilling and wood-using industries in eastern Canada; second, the Vancouver laboratory, which is conducting studies and tests affecting this 5849-36] i
industry in the western coastal region; and third, the Montreal laboratory at McGill University, operated by the pulp and paper research institute of Canada under a joint agreement between the dominion government, the Canadian pulp and paper association and McGill University, which serves the pulp and paper industry only.
I might mention some of the work carried on at the Ottawa laboratory. There is the division of timber mechanics; the division of wood chemistry; the division of wood utilization and lumber seasoning; the division of wood preservation and timber pathology; and publications.
Is this a grant to the forestry branch of the University of British Columbia?

The University of
British Columbia provides the space on the campus and we provide the buildings and personnel to carry on the work.

You make no financial grant, in the same way as you make a grant to McGill University?
'Mr. MacKINNON: That is scarcely a good comparison, because the work at McGill is being carried on by the pulp and paper industry, McGill university and the dominion government. There is no direct grant for this purpose to the University of British Columbia at the present time.
The timber industries in British Columbia make a grant to the University of British Columbia. I hope that the government will consider doing the same thing next year.

I should like to offer a suggestion to the minister, because of the deep interest in this subject on the part of a number of the people I represent. I understand that the forestry branch of the government of Sweden, which carries on similar investigations, is in the habit of keeping in close touch with the development of logging and sawmill machinery, and other machinery allied to the lumber industry, and that in northern Europe there have been developed in recent years some efficient small sawmill units and things of that type which are not in use in Canada at the present time. I am just offering the minister the suggestion that our forest products research branch, or some branch working closely with it, should give some attention to that subject, so that these newer ideas may be brought more quickly to the attention of our lumber operators and people interested in the forest industry.

Item agreed to.

Mines, forests and scientific services branch- Eastern Rockies forest conservation board-
171. To provide for the salaries and expenses of dominion members of the board and their alternates and sundry expenses in connection with the maintenance and operation of the Ottawa office of the board, $30,000.

Will the minister please explain this item, especially in view of the next item, which is for the sum of $175,000? The details given for this item simply show-amounts for temporary assistance and travelling expenses, and do not show anything for the salaries of the members of the board. How many members are on this board, and what salaries are paid?

The board consists of three members, two appointed by the dominion government and one by the province of Alberta. I believe the chairman, General Kennedy, receives a salary of $12,000 a year. The other appointee of the dominion government is Mr. Wardle, of the Department of Mines and Resources. He is a civil servant, who receives no special salary for this work. At the moment I do not remember the representative of the province of Alberta or his salary.

Where doe3 General
Kennedy's salary appear? I see only $12,000 for temporary assistance.
This vote provides for the salary of the chairman of the board, for the travelling expenses of the chairman and the other dominion member, and for the maintenance and operation of the Ottawa office.
But it just shows temporary assistance; that is what I am getting at. What do you pay the permanent members of the board, and where is that shown in these estimates?
The chairman of the board is not a civil servant.
Then where would he get his salary?
Out of this sum we are voting.
There is $12,000 for temporary assistance. Does that represent the salary of the chairman of the board? That is what I should like to know.
Yes.

Item agreed to.

Mines, forests and scientific services branch- Eastern Rockies forest conservation boards-
17Z. Dominion contribution towards annual maintenance, including staff and expenses, $175,000.

This has to do with the reforestation of the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains, which I have been pressing for some years and which I am glad to see now is under way. Last year, if I remember rightly, we voted a total of some $6,000,000 to be expended over a number of years. Last fall, on a call to the bureau of reclamation offices in Denver to inquire into what they are doing on the eastern slopes of their mountains, where they are reforesting, I learned something which may indicate one of the causes of the excessive floods in British Columbia. I learned that forest fires in the United States had a serious effect on the watersheds of the big rivers there, because the accumulation of soot from the burning fires prevented the growth of the glaciers, which is most important. These fires strip off the forests, and the result is that the run-off is much more rapid than it otherwise would be. I have been wondering whether that is not one of the causes of the rapid runoff in the British Columbia watersheds.
I notice that this vote is just for the eastern slope of the Rockies. The destruction in the Fraser river watershed is about 30,000 acres a year. In ten years this means that 300,000 acres of forest have been destroyed. This means that the winter accumulation will run off much more rapidly than it otherwise would. This was one of the major causes of the terrible floods in the Fraser valley. There should be a vote, at least by next year, for the reforestation of the slopes of the Rocky mountains in the Fraser river watershed.
I am all for this vote, having promoted this matter for years. I simply ask if it would not be well to make an investigation of the Fraser river watershed to see if the floods which they have had this year and which are higher than in any recorded year in the past, are not partly the result of the denuding of the mountain slopes.

The problem of the western slope of the Rockies is a problem for British Columbia; the problem of the eastern slope becomes a problem of the dominion government inasmuch as the water supply of three provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, is affected.

I outlined all that when the bill was going through, but I am going to ask the minister to consider the reforestation of the slopes in the Fraser river watershed that

Supply-Mines and Resources
have been burned off. It is a dominion matter, because we have agreed to pay half the expenses of the results of the floods.
We are now and have been working on an investigation of the Columbia river watershed in conjunction with the United States, but I shall give consideration to what the hon. member has said.
Why is that work being done on the Columbia river watershed?
It is an international matter.
Is it the intention to undertake forest conservation measures in any other part of Canada than the eastern slope of the Rockies?
We can initiate such undertakings only in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon and the national parks; the initiation of a project of that kind elsewhere would have to be by the province.
Would the dominion be willing to enter into a scheme, say with the province of British Columbia, of forest conservation?
I can always discuss it with my colleagues.
Is the dominion in a position to enter into negotiations with the province for forest conservation?

If British Columbia, which owns its own natural resources, including the timber resources, came to the dominion government with a proposal for joint control of some kind, consideration would be given. I do not think anything further can be said.

Although it has not been mentioned, it is an obvious matter that a large percentage of the forest fires, which do great damage in Alberta, originate in British Columbia. That is no reflection upon British Columbia; it is just the fact. How can we take care of forest fires in Alberta unless there is some provision for co-operating with British Columbia in taking care of forest fires when they are just beginning?
It seems to me to be somewhat inconsistent to say that the problem belongs to British Columbia when the eastern slope of the Rockies is a dominion concern because it affects three provinces. Fires in British Columbia affect two provinces, and perhaps three. A forest fire starts in British Columbia, gets out of control and' crosses the Alberta border where we are completely unable to handle it. It seems to me that the minister should take a more far-reaching and long-range attitude toward this whole matter of forest conservation.

Having seen a forest fire, I should like to ask a question. Is it not a fact that there is no way of stopping a forest fire that has got going, except by rain or a change in the wind? You can go up behind a fire with your buckets and gas engines, but all you can do is to try to see that it will not start again.
The second thing I want to ask is this. If the dominion and the provinces are going into fire prevention, would there not be a complete duplication of effort? If you are referring to contributions, that is an entirely different matter; but would it not be extravagant to have side by side a dominion fire protection service and a provincial fire prevention service?

What has been said by the hon. member for Calgary West is a statement of fact rather than a question. I do not think there is any doubt but that once a large fire gets rolling, it is practically impossible to stop it, except by rain or by har ing it. burn itself out.

I am glad the hon. member for Calgary West mentioned this matter, because it gives me a chance to clarify my position. I am not stupid enough to suppose that the dominion government should set up an independent fire prevention service, but the dominion government could co-operate with the provinces in much the same way that it has co-operated with British Columbia in connection with the floods. Canada did not have a flood prevention service in British Columbia; all we did was to assure British Columbia that we would be behind them in everything they intended to do.
Did the dominion government take any part in fighting the forest fires which have raged recently in Ontario?
They are still going.
The dominion government did not participate except in our own reserves.
Did Ontario seek the assistance of the dominion government?
I am told not.
If they had done so, would the dominion government have been prepared to help them?
The dominion government lent planes to Ontario to help with the dry ice proposition.

I just want to get some information. Along with others, I have been here for thirteen years and have been greatly
Supply-Mines and Resources

dissatisfied over the fact that apparently nothing is being done to take care of our forests. We have only one set of forests; when they are devastated, we shall have no forests, and the next generation will not be in anything like as fortunate a position with respect to forests as we are. That is a position which ought not to exist. In Germany and many European countries they take the greatest care to see that every time a tree is cut down, another is planted in the ground in its place. If we would use anything like husbandry in respect of our forests we would have a magnificent assest for a thousand years for coming generations. What I should like to see is something done right away, not twenty-five years from now after the forests have been largely destroyed. I should like to see a start made tomorrow. Has the minister any intention or idea of starting such activities?

The province of Ontario is already doing for itself all the things the hon. member has mentioned and is spending its own money in doing it. Why duplicate the work? You would have the dominion and the provincial fire-fighters falling over themselves, each trying to do the same job. Why spend the taxpayers' money twice?
That remark is utter nonsense. To say that Ontario has done all it possibly could is sheer tommy-rot.
That is a matter of opinion.

If Ontario does not need help I may tell the chairman and the committee that Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan do. They have not as much money to spend, but have relatively as many forests to take care of as Ontario.
Earlier this evening I stated that the dominion is in touch with the other provinces, Ontario for one, for the purpose of making a study of the most scientific methods of fire protection.

Has any progress
been made? What has actually been done besides getting in touch?

What steps does the federal government take to protect its own forest lands against fire? There are thousands of acres of dominion-owned forest lands in British Columbia, on Indian reserves and elsewhere. What steps does the federal government take to protect dominion forests?

The dominion government is using the best methods known to safeguard the forests in the parks and on other

dominion-owned lands. There is an extensive system comprising fire rangers, look-out towers and water stations all through our national parks.

Item agreed to.

Will it be distributed before the end of the session?

temporary assistance is down. I am inclined to think there has been a cut in this service rather than an increase.

I am informed that a ground crew' is there now.

Item agreed to.

Surveys and mapping bureau-
175. Surveys and mapping bureau administration, $14,590.

On several occasions I have complained about mapping. The present minister, who W'as then in another department, corrected what I complained of at that time. Item agreed to.
Mines, forests and scientific surveys branch- Surveys and mapping bureau-
177. Canadian hydrographic service, $2,364,941.

It is utterly impossible at this stage of the session to inquire exhaustively into such large expenditures. I notice that, of this 82,361,911, approximately 81,600,000 is for materials and equipment. Obviously we cannot get the list of that at the present time. Then I note that about $400,000 is for temporary assistance and wages. Why is there such a large amount earmarked for temporary assistance?
This item looks large, but hon. members must remember that provision is made for the purchase and fitting of two hydrographic ships.

For a considerable period of time there has been dissatisfaction among the crews of two hydrographic ships on the w'est coast, the William J. Stewart and the Parry. It came to a climax last month when they were asked to sign at last year's wages, which w-ere $27 to $40 less than the wages that were paid on government ships of the same kind for -the same ratings on the east coast. Some adjustment was made. Have the wages been brought up now, so that they are comparable with wages paid on the east coast? Have the crews signed on to the satisfaction of all concerned?

The wages were
adjusted through the joint efforts of this department and the Department of Labour. I am informed that the men have all signed on and that the rates are satisfactory.

A good deal of difficulty was experienced last summer in maintaining these ships. There was a tremendous turnover of personnel. That was largely on account of living conditions on the William J. Stewart. Is any provision made in this item for the improvement of living conditions, general layout, messing quarters, galleys and so forth on that vessel?
I am informed that improvements were made in living conditions on the William J. Stewart. I have not the details, but improvements were made.
Structural improvements?
I am sorry, I have not the details.

I should like to revert to item 176 for a moment, which was passed over. It includes the expenses of the geographic board of Canada. What were the expenses of the geographic board of Canada? Who are the members of the board? What do their duties
Supply-Mines and Resources

consist of? What policy is followed in naming mountains, lakes and natural features under their jurisdiction?

It is impossible for me at the present time to give all the information asked for by the hon. member for Kootenay East as to the membership of the geographic board. I notice there is an increase of over SI,500,000 with respect to the hydrographic service. I am not begrudging the increase. I was wondering why the increase. Have we undertaken more extensive services than in the past?
I have just explained that the large increase in the vote is caused by the purchase of two ships at a cost of $1,500,000.

Does
the international peace garden come under the jurisdiction of this department?
To what peace garden does my hon. friend refer, the one south of Brandon?
Yes.

It does not come under the parks branch of this department. No decision will be
reached in that respect, I hope, without reference to the province of British Columbia, because of the vital importance of this to certain industries there.

Is the province of British Columbia consulted, or is it merely informed of what is done by the dominion? The provincial government is veiy much concerned in the issue.

I was going to ask the minister a question of which I am sure he would not have knowledge. Perhaps his officials can tell him if there is a report of the international joint commission in connection with the diversion of the water from Chamberlain lake in Maine, which is one of the main sources of the Allagash river which flows into the St. John river and is therefore in the international watershed, in which water is diverted out of Chamberlain lake within the St. John river watershed into the Penobscot watershed in Maine. The farmers in the district there living along the banks have their grain seeded and, when the waters are let out with such great force, the river sometimes rises five or six feet, backing up and flooding out the farmers in the district. replaced by a temporary officer, but I notice that the salaries of at least three of the scientists employed in that observatory have apparently been reduced, because the amount provided is less than that .provided last year for these particular individuals. 191i. Lands division-administration of dominion, ordnance and admiralty and public lands; seed grain collections, $197,885.

I see that seed grain collections come under this item.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee the matter of the old outstanding 1914-1923 seed grain relief. The answer to a question on the order paper shows that $10,132,640 was given out by the federal government between 1914 and 1923 for seed relief; that $8,417,887 was paid back; that $1,432,900 in interest was paid back, leaving an unpaid balance of principal and interest of $1,431,003 and $1,652,009 respectively. That was as of March 31, 1948. It further shows that no notices of this account were sent out by the government since 1930; that is eighteen years ago. It shows further that the bookkeeping in connection with this account cost $22,000 to keep it open.
Most of this relief was given out in 1914. I would say that not over fifteen per cent of
the people who received this relief are now residing on the land. A great part of this land is today held under grazing lease, or has gone back in what is called "gone-back preemption." I should like to point out to the committee that between 1923 and 1938 all the relief given out was cancelled by the governments concerned. The Saskatchewan government on its own responsibility cancelled 50 per cent of the 1938 seed relief.
In view of these facts, I should like to say to the minister, first, that in my opinion this account is a dead horse, having regard to any equity that is left in the land against which the relief is charged; second, that it was considered to be almost a national emergency in the years that this relief was given out; third, that eighty-five per cent of the people who received that relief are either dead or have left the land; fourth, that this seed and relief has been cancelled in every province, and I do not see why the federal government hangs on to this old item, at some cost in keeping the accounts. A question placed on the order paper asked the cost to the federal treasury of keeping this account open since 1945, and the answer was 822,000. I believe it would be a good thing to wipe off this amount, and I would ask the minister to give that suggestion his serious consideration. Perhaps he would care to make some comment on it.
Mr. 8INNOTT:	If the province of
Saskatchewan will pay it off, we will wipe out the bookkeeping item.
This matter has been submitted in the past to committees of which I have been a member, and I shall be glad to give it further consideration.

At Cat lake, which is about thirty miles northeast of Lac du Bonnet.

Does the minister know whether a monument or any other marking is to be erected to the late Lucy Maude Montgomery? I understand that this has 
been brought to the attention of the historic sites committee, and I should like to know whether any action is to be taken in this respect.
I believe the historic sites committee has under consideration the placing of what is called a marker at the home of the late Lucy Maude Montgomery.
There is an increase here of nearly $5,000,000. Would the minister have something to say about that?
What land was purchased, and what was the price?

I mentioned that as yet I have not had an opportunity to see the magazine.
How much is it proposed to spend this year on the park in New Brunswick; what will be the nature of the work, and how many men will be employed?

I asked the minister what land was purchased and at what price, and what buildings were purchased, and at what prices, for this $4,894,000.

For how much?
I have no idea.
There must be some figure, because we have the amount of $4,894,000 this year.

acquired by the province of New Brunswick and transferred to the dominion, free of charge.
But the explanation given is, "Acquisition of land and/or construction of buildings, works and structures, $4,894,210." What does the government get for that amount of money?

Riding	Mountain	 487,500

Last year I was in Dawson and I had an opportunity to look over some of the old landmarks in that town. There is just one of the old dance halls left, this particular one having been built in 1898 or 1899. I found it of great interest to go through that.

Did you see the
photographs?

I should like to see that dance hall restored. If it were in Skag-way they would have Dan McGrew lying out in the middle of the hall and would be making a fortune out of it. If that old dance hall were saved, when the highways opened up, United States tourists would be flocking in and hundreds of thousands of United States dollars would be kept in this country. It would be of great interest to those people. This i3 part of our history and every child has read about it.

I was not asking the hon. member if he had seen any postcards;
I was asking him if he had seen the painting of the Floradora sextette that is in that hall?
Has a grant been made to the Bell homestead at Brantford, the Mohawk church, or the birthplace of Pauline Johnson?
I shall have to get that information for the hon. member.

There is to be a great increase in the expenditures on national parks.
I am particularly interested in Prince Albert national park, because so many of the people from my constituency go there for their summer holidays. I understand that Jasper and Prince Albert parks are to share in a road building program. I should like to know the nature of the top surfacing and for what length of road the improvements will be made?
The main road in Prince Albert park is being prepared for hard surfacing.
Is that the road in the park or the road leading to the park?
In all cases the road work is being done within the parks.
Will the asphalt construction be carried out this year?
Not this year.
Is the minister planning to build housing of any type in that park?
No housing program is contemplated.

I hope that the minister will see that the people in the low-income brackets are taken care of. I am thinking particularly of the shack tenters and ordinary tenters who, in the past, did not receive sympathetic treatment from the former superintendent. While I had to condemn the attitude of the superintendent who was there last year toward these people, I want to commend the attitude of the present superintendent. I understand that he is a great improvement over the last man. Is lumber still being cut by a private company at a nominal fee inside Riding Mountain park?

I am informed that the shack-town space in Prince Albert park is being increased this year. The policy of providing attractions for people in the lower income groups is being emphasized throughout all our parks. I am informed that an old timber

licence was in operation at the time the Riding Mountain park was established and some timber is still being taken out.

How long is that contract likely to go on? I understand that that company has the privilege of cutting timber in perpetuity, that it is permitted to go in and cut anything that is saleable. I do not want to be sarcastic, but I hope that the government has no reforestation program for that particular park, because they would be simply reforesting so that a private company might continue to cut. There has been a tremendous exploitation of the timber on our common land and surely, when some of those lands are enclosed as a national park, there should be some way to stop this iniquitous-I used that word advisedly-contract.
I am informed that we are reducing the size of the timber 'imits as cutting operations take place.

Perhaps the hon. member for Kamloops would be satisfied if we

gave him a breakdown for one of the parks, say Banff or Jasper. I cannot do so right now.

speechtext: Put the breakdown on the record tomorrow.

that tomorrow, for Banff park.
For the whole thing.
I am sure hon. members do not realize how much detail they are asking for. It would fill pages of Hansard to put the whole breakdown on the record. I am suggesting a sample breakdown.

Could the minister not tell us how much in each of the parks will be spent for roads, how much for buildings, how much for salaries, how much for new construction or work not previously done in the parks? The figures could be grouped under main headings, so that we would have some idea of what new work is being undertaken.

All the detail that is given of the $2,300,000 for Jasper is that it is for land and the construction of buildings. Surely we can be given more details than that.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
